passage: I'm Ayesha, and I sit behind Keerthana. When the science tests came back, she got 14 out of 20 and smiled. Then she turned and saw Chandni's paper: 20 out of 20, with a star. Keerthana's smile dropped. She folded her paper in half so no one could see and put her head on the desk. At break she didn't eat her idli. Then Ma'am said, "This was a hard test. The class average was only 9." Keerthana sat straight up and unfolded her paper. "Fourteen is five more than average!" she told me, grinning. I don't know exactly what she felt. But the paper said 14 the whole time.

qa.q: What was the class average?
qa.a: Only 9.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana fold her paper after seeing Chandni's mark?
qa.a: Next to Chandni's 20 with a star, her 14 suddenly felt bad, so she seemed embarrassed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What could Keerthana ask herself next time before reacting to a friend's mark?
qa.a: She could ask what she understood and what she missed, judging her 14 by her own learning instead of by whoever sits nearby.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Keerthana's change of mood?

passage:
Monday: Rashmi got 32 out of 50 in maths and felt fine. It was more than last time.
Tuesday: At lunch, Yash said he got 48. "Only two wrong!" Rashmi pushed her rice around. At home she told Amma she was "the worst at maths in the whole world" and wouldn't show her the paper.
Thursday: Sir wrote the class scores on the board, without names. Most were in the twenties. Rashmi counted. Hers was the fifth highest. She ran home, slapped the paper on the table and said, "Amma, I'm actually good!" Amma looked at the paper. It was the same 32 Rashmi had refused to show her on Tuesday.

qa.q: How many marks did Rashmi get in maths?
qa.a: 32 out of 50.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling on Tuesday when she called herself "the worst at maths"?
qa.a: She felt miserable and ashamed, because Yash's 48 made her own 32 look tiny.

qa.q: What could Amma say on Thursday to help Rashmi next time?
qa.a: She could point out gently that it's the same 32, and ask how it compares with Rashmi's own last test, so her feelings rest on her own progress, not only on others' marks.

qa.q: How might Yash feel if he knew his "Only two wrong!" upset Rashmi?
qa.a: Yash was just happy about his score and probably didn't mean to hurt anyone, so he might feel surprised or sorry. 😅

grounding: Across a week, a girl's feeling about the same maths score swings from content to miserable to delighted depending on whose marks she compares it with.

passage: Usha, sit here. You're sulking because your friend got more marks, na? Let me tell you about your Vishal Dadu at ten. I pulled that paper out so fast. I was a king again. Same sixty, Usha. Only the thing I held it next to had changed.

qa.q: What did Bhola get in the exam?

qa.q: Why did young Vishal hide the paper under his mattress?
qa.a: Next to Bhola's ninety-five, his sixty felt like a stone, so he felt ashamed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What choice could young Vishal have made on the way home that might have saved his dinner?
qa.a: He could have held on to how pleased he was before Bhola showed his paper, or found out how the rest of the class did before deciding his sixty was bad.

qa.q: Why might Dadu be telling Usha this story now?
qa.a: Usha is sulking over a friend's higher marks, and Dadu wants to show, through his own boyhood, that the feeling depends on what the marks are compared with.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, the same exam score felt shameful beside a friend's mark and wonderful once he heard the class did worse.

passage:
Rain lashed the school hall, and the fans were so loud that the teacher had to shout out the science marks one by one. Anjali heard hers: 18 out of 25. She smiled.
Then Sudha, beside her, got 25. Everyone clapped. Anjali's smile slipped. Her 18 suddenly felt like a fail. She stared at the wet windows and felt her throat go tight.
At the end, the teacher shouted, "Most of you did badly. The class average is only 12!"
Anjali sat up. Twelve! Her 18 was way above that. She turned to Sudha, grinning. "I did well, na?"
"You did," said Sudha.
Walking home under one umbrella, Anjali thought about how her mark had gone from good to terrible to great in ten minutes, and never changed once.

qa.q: What was the class average in the science test?
qa.a: The class average is only 12.

qa.q: Why did Anjali's throat go tight after Sudha's mark?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and small, because next to Sudha's 25 her own 18 suddenly seemed like a fail.

qa.q: What could Anjali remind herself the next time a friend gets a higher mark?
qa.a: She could compare her mark with her own last score or with what she learned, instead of only with her friend's.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Anjali asks "I did well, na?"
qa.a: Sudha may feel glad to share the moment and relieved that Anjali is happy again.

grounding: A student with a fair mark feels bad after a friend's full score, then delighted when the class average is announced as low.
